question.problem: A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ represents a dilation. Given that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242551/assets/4839ef0c15f8fae5c216d7e9121e03a1cde80804f55d92da3fc5e342a3de016e.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14242551/assets/d0bb86720d4b08e89ad108b90b603421d7c0011b903ff1eef17856a4f061cdc3.svg) what is the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}?$
question.worked_solution:
We can write $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot [\begin{aligned}24 \\ 16\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}v\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{v},$ we conclude that the linear transformation $\mathbf T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k = \dfrac{1}{4}.$
